analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans covering childbirth to pay for a minimum hospital stay of 48 hours after birth.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee; it died at the end of the session without a hearing or vote, despite its sponsor and 19 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1996, health insurers and HMOs were pushing new mothers and newborns out of the hospital within a day or two of delivery, a practice critics called 'drive-through deliveries.' This bill would have required any insurer, HMO, or employer health plan that covers childbirth to cover at least 48 hours in the hospital after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean section, plus follow-up care if the mother leaves early. Plans that refused would have owed a tax equal to 25% of their premiums. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Mothers and newborns with job-based or private health insurance. They would be guaranteed coverage for a longer hospital stay after delivery, or a home visit and follow-up care if they and their doctor choose an early discharge. Plans would also be barred from offering mothers money to leave early or cutting payments to doctors who keep mothers in the hospital.

how_it_helps.text: Plans covering childbirth must pay for at least 48 hours of inpatient care after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean section.
If a mother is discharged early, the plan must cover follow-up care at home or in a clinic by a nurse, doctor, nurse midwife, or similar provider within 72 hours of discharge.
Plans may not pay mothers to leave early, penalize doctors who keep mothers hospitalized, or deny coverage to a mother and newborn who use the minimum stay.
Insurers or HMOs that fail to meet the requirements face a tax of 25% of the premiums they collect; employer plans face a tax of 25% of their health benefit spending.
The bill does not override stronger state protections, and it does not force any mother to stay in the hospital against her and her doctor's judgment.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, HMOs, and employers who fund group health plans, through longer hospital stays that are built into premiums and benefit costs. Working families would bear part of this through somewhat higher premiums, in exchange for the guaranteed stay.

drawbacks.text: A fixed 48- or 96-hour floor is a one-size-fits-all rule; longer stays add real cost, and the bill itself concedes that the right length of care varies with each mother's health, her baby's condition, and her support at home.
The enforcement mechanism is blunt: a tax equal to 25% of a noncomplying plan's entire annual premiums, rather than a penalty scaled to the violation.
The added coverage would be reflected in insurance premiums paid by employers and workers, so the mandate's cost does not disappear; it is spread across everyone buying coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit is concrete and targeted: newborns discharged within hours of birth face risks of undetected jaundice, dehydration, and other problems that a longer stay or a nurse's home visit can catch. The cost is a modest premium increase spread across everyone with coverage. The bill's main design weakness is the blunt 25%-of-premiums tax and the fixed hourly floor, though it wisely lets a mother and her doctor choose early discharge with covered follow-up care instead of forcing a fixed stay.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the session ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 9, 1996 by Rep. Gerald Kleczka with 18 original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place; the only further action in the record is a second set of the sponsor's introductory remarks on May 24, 1996.
The bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, HMOs, and employers funding group health plans were better off in the short run because they avoided the 48-hour mandate and the 25% tax under this bill. New mothers ultimately got essentially the same minimum-stay protections anyway, when Congress enacted a nearly identical law later in 1996, but this bill itself died without a vote.

for.name: Rep. Gerald Kleczka
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor twice in May 1996.

for.name: 19 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Stark, Rangel, Cardin, McDermott, and Levin.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote; it remained in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; it never received a hearing or vote in 1996.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill. Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat, while the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee simply took no action, so opposition ran along party control rather than any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill forces plans covering childbirth to pay for 48- or 96-hour stays and follow-up care, and threatens a tax of 25% of premiums for noncompliance. Insurers were managing costs by pushing quick post-birth discharges, which this bill would end.
Plan sponsors would owe a tax of 25% of plan health expenditures if they fail to meet the minimum-stay rules, raising the cost of job-based coverage.
Longer guaranteed post-delivery stays mean more billed inpatient days for hospitals that deliver babies, alongside the health benefit to mothers and newborns.
Doctors, nurse midwives, and nurses would be paid for longer stays or covered home visits, and the bill bars plans from cutting their reimbursement for following the rules.
